The TBC life prediction modeling work was divided into two phases: Phase I focused on failure analysis and developing preliminary models, while Phase II aimed to produce design-capable models.
The TBC life prediction modeling work involved contracts with Pratt & Whitney, GE, and Garrett, as well as a grant with Cleveland State University and in-house efforts at NASA.

Key accomplishments of the TBC work in FY 1986 included the development and initial verification of a preliminary life model by Pratt & Whitney, determination of coating mechanical and thermal properties, elucidation of failure mechanisms, finite element modeling of stresses, evaluation of NDE methods, and an engine test conducted by Garrett.
The goal of the airfoil deposition modeling work was to develop and verify a model to predict the quantity and location of corrodant deposition on turbine airfoils.

The key accomplishments of the airfoil deposition modeling work included verification of the chemically frozen boundary layer (CFBL) theory and encouraging results with the recently developed local thermochemical equilibrium (LTCE) theory, which agreed within 7% in predicting deposition rates.

The rig/engine correlation work aimed to provide a unique and relatively inexpensive laboratory to aid in the development of environment attack life prediction tools for hot section materials, by verifying advances made in life prediction at pressure levels encountered in gas turbine engines.
The TBC mechanical behavior work, conducted through a grant with Cleveland State University, focused on modeling the residual stresses in TBCs.

The high-pressure burner rig development work was aimed at providing a laboratory capability to complement the contract efforts, by enabling high-heat flux tests to study failure mechanisms and model verification.

The key elements of the TBC life prediction modeling approach were failure mechanisms analysis, mechanical behavior modeling, life model development, and model verification, all with the goal of enabling the use of TBCs in the 'prime mode' on aircraft engine components.
The full benefits of TBCs can only be achieved when it becomes possible to use them in the 'prime-reliant' mode, where an uncoated airfoil cannot survive the temperatures encountered.
TBC life prediction models combined with other advances in coatings technology will be required before designers will be willing to use TBCs in the prime reliant mode.
The TBC life modeling contracts are divided into two phases, with each of the three contractors currently in the third and final year of Phase I.
The output of Phase I will be a preliminary model, while the output of Phase II will be a design-capable model.

The TBC life prediction modeling strategy involves studying failure mechanisms, mechanical behavior, and model verification, in order to develop a comprehensive life prediction model suitable for the 'prime mode' use of TBCs.
The in-house rig/engine correlation work is aimed at high pressure burner rig development to complement the contract efforts.
